title: The Gurus' teachings close
hookLine: five Gurus, one signature: looking back at Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan and Tegh Bahadur

lines: MAHALA ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR, FIVE, NINE.
LISTEN TO THEM ALL AT ONCE.
cards: Here's a small thing on the page that's easy to miss. When the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, they use one name: Nanak. Guru Angad signs as Nanak.
So do Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, and the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. How do readers tell them apart? Above each hymn sits a heading: Mahala, with a number.
One, two, three, four, five, nine. Different hands, different generations, one name. Today closes this stretch of the path by listening to them all at once.

teach.b: Start with Guru Angad, the quiet successor. Few words, deep. He called the Guru a light where all was dark, warned against service mixed with pride, and called ego an illness with the cure inside it.

teach.h: AMAR DAS AND RAM DAS: LIGHT, KITCHEN, CITY.
teach.b: Then Guru Amar Das: O mind, you are the form of light. The world is burning; save it by any door. Not the pyre, but a faithful life.
And a kitchen open to all. Then Guru Ram Das: the Gursikh's morning, rising early, remembering, then going to work still remembering. Wedding songs of the soul riding to the Beloved.
A city where the market itself could be holy.

teach.h: ARJAN AND THE NINTH: SWEET, LEVEL, REMAINING.
teach.b: Then Guru Arjan: an alphabet that ends in grace, a plate of truth, contentment and reflection, what You do seems sweet to me, serving the One, and a book chosen carefully, with room for saints from outside the line of Gurus.
And last, the ninth Guru: neither fear nor frighten, home held lightly, their faith, their right, level, a dream, a bubble, and the Name that remains.
Hear how different they sound: a spare one-liner, a burning world, a wedding song, a long alphabet, a calm verse tradition hears through his last days.
And yet it's one teaching: the One, the Name, the turning from ego toward the Guru.
Sikhs hear that oneness in the shared signature, Nanak, and speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru, the way a lamp lights a lamp.
The flame looks different in each lamp. It's the same flame.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib each Guru's hymns carry a Mahala heading with a number, and are signed Nanak; Sikhs read and sing them together as one Guru's word.

games.q: what does “the gurus' teachings close” mean?
o: the final hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib
a look back at five Gurus' voices as one teaching
the day the last human Guru closed the scripture

games.q: the Guru and the voice: tap the pairs.
p: what You do seems sweet to me

s: each Guru signs his hymns with his own name
they sign as Nanak; the Mahala heading tells readers which Guru it is.
Mahala nine marks the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur
the ninth Guru; his hymns and saloks sit in the Granth with the earlier Gurus'.
the Gurus' different styles mean different teachings
different voices, one teaching: the One, the Name, the turning from ego.

games.q: you're the second Guru, writing your first hymn. how do you sign it?
games.why: the Gurus sign as Nanak; Sikhs speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru, like a lamp lighting a lamp.

practice: Let the five Gurus pass by one at a time, like singers taking turns: Guru Angad, short and sharp; Guru Amar Das, the open kitchen; Guru Ram Das, the morning; Guru Arjan, sweetness; Guru Tegh Bahadur, the level heart.
Notice which voice you lean toward, with no wrong answer, and hold one line of theirs to come back to. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: The Gurus' teachings close. From the second Guru to the fifth, and the ninth: different voices, one signature, one teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: the heading over the Gurus' hymns, with a number telling which Guru: Mahala one is Guru Nanak.

carryVoice: Your line: one teaching, many voices. Next come the tenth Guru's writings. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Mahala headings and the signature Nanak in hymns of Mahala 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9
